title: THE MOTHER WHO NAMED HER SON “NO GLORY”
paragraphs: THE MOTHER WHO NAMED HER SON “NO GLORY”
She was dying. Her husband was dead. Israel had been shattered. Yet the tragedy that broke her heart most deeply was something many Christians today barely notice when it happens: the glory was gone.
There are names a mother whispers because she has dreamed of them for years.
Names spoken over a swollen belly.
Names written secretly on paper.
Names carrying prayers, hopes, inheritance, promise.
And then there is the name one dying mother gave her newborn son.
Ichabod.
A name forever attached to one of the darkest days in Israel’s history.
A name commonly understood along the lines of “No glory,” “Where is the glory?” or “Alas, the glory.”
But Scripture itself tells us exactly what was crushing this woman’s soul.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 4:21 says:
וַתִּקְרָא לַנַּעַר אִיכָבוֹד לֵאמֹר גָּלָה כָבוֹד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
Vattiqra lanna'ar I-khavod lemor: galah khavod mi-Yisrael.
“She named the boy Ichabod, saying, ‘The glory has departed from Israel.’”
גָּלָה כָבוֹד — galah kavod.
The glory has departed.
The verb גָּלָה — galah can carry the sense of going away, being removed, or going into exile.
And כָּבוֹד — kavod, “glory,” comes from a Hebrew word-family associated with weight or heaviness and, by extension, honor, splendor, significance, and glory.
In other words, this was not merely a woman saying, “Something bad happened today.”
Something weighty had been lost.
And if you understand why, this ancient mother’s final words may expose something terrifying about modern Christianity—and perhaps something about your own heart.
Because the tragedy of 1 Samuel 4 did not begin when Israel lost a battle.
It began when people learned how to carry the things of God while their hearts were drifting from the God those things represented.
That should frighten us more than losing money.
More than losing influence.
More than losing popularity.
More than losing comfort.
Because it is possible to keep the religious language while losing reverence.
Possible to sing worship songs while protecting secret sin.
Possible to quote Scripture while refusing to obey it.
Possible to know how church works while barely knowing what trembling before a holy God feels like anymore.
Israel discovered this painfully.
Before Ichabod was born, the spiritual condition of Israel was already diseased.

Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests, but their behavior dishonored the LORD. They abused their priestly position, treated the LORD's offering with contempt, and persisted in sexual immorality around the sanctuary.
They had proximity to holy things without holy hearts.
That is one of Scripture's most terrifying warnings.
You can stand near an altar and still be far from God.
You can hold a Bible and still resist its Author.
You can have Christian content filling your phone while lust, bitterness, greed, pride, unforgiveness, hypocrisy, or secret compromise is quietly consuming your soul.
You can even become skilled at appearing spiritually alive.
And then Israel went to war.
They were defeated by the Philistines.
Thousands died.
But instead of first asking what their defeat revealed about their relationship with God, Israel reached for something religious.
The ark.
“Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD,” they essentially reasoned, so that it might save them from their enemies.
Do you see the danger?
They wanted God's power without confronting their rebellion.
They wanted victory without repentance.
They wanted the symbol of God's presence without surrendering to the God whose presence made it holy.
The ark was not a magical object.
God could not be manipulated.
Yet Israel treated what was sacred almost like a spiritual weapon they could deploy whenever life became desperate.
And we are capable of doing the same thing.
We ignore God until the diagnosis comes.
Then we pray.
We compromise until the marriage starts collapsing.
Then we pray.
We feed an addiction privately until its consequences become public.
Then we pray.
We build our lives around ourselves, sprinkle Christian language over our ambitions, and when everything begins falling apart we suddenly reach for God as though He were an emergency lever.
Prayer is good.
Running to God is good.
The prodigal is always right to come home.
But there is a difference between desperately wanting God and desperately wanting God to remove the consequences while we keep the idols.
Israel carried the ark into battle.
The people shouted so loudly that the earth shook.
Imagine the scene.
Thousands of voices.
Religious excitement.
Confidence.
Noise.
The visible symbol of God's covenant presence standing among them.
It probably looked like revival.
Then the Philistines attacked.
Israel was crushed.
Thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fell.
Hophni died.
Phinehas died.
And the ark of God was captured.
A messenger ran from the battlefield to Shiloh with his clothes torn and dust upon his head.
Eli was waiting.
Scripture says his heart trembled for the ark of God.
Then the report came.
Israel has fled.
Your sons are dead.
The ark has been captured.
When Eli heard about the ark, the old priest fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died.
But the story was not finished.
Somewhere nearby was Phinehas's pregnant wife.
Imagine what reached her ears in a matter of moments.
Her nation had suffered catastrophic defeat.
Her husband was dead.
Her brother-in-law was dead.
Her father-in-law was dead.
The ark of God had been captured.
The shock sent her into labor.
She gave birth while dying.
Women stood around her trying desperately to give her one reason to hold on.
“Do not be afraid. You have given birth to a son.”
Normally those words should have pierced darkness with joy.
A son.
Life arriving while death surrounded her.
A future.
A reason to smile.
But Scripture says she did not answer.
She did not set her heart upon it.
Her body was fading.
And then she named him.
Ichabod.
Not because her husband was dead alone.
Not because Eli was dead alone.
Not simply because Israel lost a battle.
Her final explanation keeps returning to the ark.
גָּלָה כָבוֹד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
Galah kavod mi-Yisrael.
“The glory has departed from Israel.”
Then Scripture repeats her final thought:
גָּלָה כָבוֹד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל כִּי נִלְקַח אֲרוֹן הָאֱלֹהִים
“The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured.”
And she died.
A baby entered the world carrying the vocabulary of a national spiritual catastrophe.
Every time someone called his name, the tragedy would echo again.
Ichabod.
Where is the glory?
No glory.
The glory has departed.
But here is where we must read the whole biblical story carefully.
The Philistines had captured the ark.
They had not captured God.
That distinction changes everything.
In the very next chapter, the Philistines put the ark inside the temple of their god Dagon.
They apparently thought Israel's God had been defeated.
Then morning came.
Dagon was lying face-down before the ark of the LORD.
They put their idol back up.
The next morning?
Dagon was down again—this time with his head and hands severed.
The message is almost impossible to miss.
Israel had been defeated.
YHWH had not.
Israel's priests had disgraced His name.
God remained holy.
The ark had been captured.
God remained sovereign.
No Philistine army had dragged the LORD into captivity.
The God of Israel did not need Israel's army to rescue Him.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs those words.
Because something has been captured in your life.
Something has died.
Something collapsed.
Maybe your marriage did not become what you prayed it would become.
Maybe your child walked away.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe the addiction returned.
Maybe you promised Jesus, “Never again,” and then found yourself crying over the same sin.
Maybe people know your Christian face but not your private war.
Maybe you look spiritually alive online while inside you keep whispering:
Where is the glory?
Where did the fire go?
Where did my hunger for Scripture go?
Why can I scroll for two hours but struggle to pray for ten minutes?
Why does temptation excite me more than holiness?
Why do I miss the person I used to be with God?
Be honest.
This may be hitting harder than you expected.
And perhaps that discomfort is mercy.
Because conviction is not Jesus throwing you away.
Conviction can be Jesus exposing what is killing you so that you will finally bring it into His light.
The answer to Ichabod is not pretending there was never a scandal.
Christianity is not a religion of pretending the scandal did not happen.
It is the announcement that God entered our scandal to redeem sinners.
And this is where the road eventually leads us far beyond Shiloh.
To Jesus Christ.
Israel's story teaches us that sacred objects cannot save sinners.
Priestly ancestry cannot save sinners.
Religious excitement cannot save sinners.
Our reputation cannot save us.
Our church attendance cannot wash away guilt.
Our good works cannot erase rebellion.
We need more than the appearance of glory.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And the Gospel declares that the eternal Son of God came to us.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He called sinners to repentance.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He exposed darkness.
He forgave.
He healed.
And then He walked willingly toward the cross.
There, something happened that makes Ichabod's story tremble with deeper significance.
Jesus cried:
Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ, λεμὰ σαβαχθανί;
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
Mark preserves the cry in transliterated Semitic form and explains it:
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Jesus was invoking Psalm 22 as He suffered on the cross.
The sinless Christ was bearing sin.
The One who deserved glory accepted shame.
The Holy One stood in the place of the guilty.
Not because the Father ceased loving the Son.
Not because the Trinity somehow broke apart.
But because at Calvary Jesus was accomplishing what no ark, priest, sacrifice of our own making, moral improvement program, or religious performance could accomplish.
Redemption.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
So the final word over everyone who comes to Christ does not have to be:
Ichabod.
Your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your eternity.
Your scandal does not have to be the end of your story.
Your adultery does not have the authority to name you forever.
Your pornography addiction does not get the final word.
Your alcoholism does not get the final word.
Your bitterness does not get the final word.
Your abortion does not get the final word.
Your prison record does not get the final word.
Your divorce does not get the final word.
Your secret compromise does not get the final word.
Your religious hypocrisy does not get the final word.
Your failure does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That does not mean sin is insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross to save us from it.
Grace is not God saying your sin never mattered.
Grace is God offering guilty sinners what we could never purchase for ourselves because Christ paid the price.
So do not turn this article into another religious object.
Do not read it, feel emotional for five minutes, press “like,” and return comfortably to the darkness Jesus is exposing.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Confess.
Stop negotiating with the sin Christ died to free you from.
If necessary, tell a mature believer what you have been hiding.
Seek accountability.
Open your Bible again.
Pray when you do not feel impressive.
Return to Christ.
Not because repentance earns salvation, but because genuine faith does not make peace with the sin that nailed our Savior to the cross.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to be painfully simple:

“Jesus, have mercy on me. I have carried Your name while protecting things that dishonor You. Forgive me. Cleanse me. I cannot rescue myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Take what I have been hiding. Teach me to follow You.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But you can stop pretending.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer in the battle.
That matters.
And there may be one person on your Facebook friends list who needs this more than you realize.
The friend who laughs all day and cries after everyone sleeps.
The husband secretly losing his spiritual fire.
The mother blaming herself for everything.
The teenager drowning in shame.
The believer who still attends church but privately wonders whether God could possibly want them back.
The person who would never search for a Christian article but might read one because you shared it.
So if this message points people faithfully toward Jesus, do not keep it imprisoned on this page.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns spiritual blessing.
It cannot.
He does not.
Jesus alone saves. Grace cannot be purchased.
Not as a transaction with God.
As mission.
Because somewhere in your circle may be an Ichabod heart.
Someone convinced the glory is gone.
Someone certain their scandal has disqualified them.
Someone who believes the worst thing they ever did has become their permanent name.
Someone standing emotionally in the ruins of Shiloh whispering:
“Where is God now?”
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them there is forgiveness for sinners.
Tell them repentance is still possible.
Tell them the cross was not reserved for respectable people.
Tell them the tomb is empty.
Tell them Christ still receives those who come to Him.
Tell them shame does not outrank grace.
Tell them failure does not outrank the blood of Jesus.
Tell them that while consequences can remain and wounds may take time to heal, Christ can make a sinner new.
Because the mother in 1 Samuel died believing she was witnessing the departure of glory.
But she could not see the chapters that were still coming.
The ark would return.
Dagon would fall.
God's purposes would continue.
David would come.
And generations later, through David's royal line, the true King would come.
Jesus.
The One of whom John would write:
καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
And John says:
ἐθεασάμεθα τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ
etheasametha tēn doxan autou.
“We have seen His glory.”
Do you see it?
Glory.
The story that seemed to scream, “The glory has departed,” is swallowed into the greater biblical story in which God's glory is revealed supremely in His Son.
Ichabod was not the last chapter.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, neither is your darkest chapter.
So repent where you need to repent.
Grieve what needs to be grieved.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Stop protecting the darkness.
Run to Christ.
And when Satan tries to name you by the chapter Jesus has forgiven, remember who has the authority to write the ending.
The scar may explain where you have been, but Jesus Christ determines who you belong to.
